This page covers the specific U.S. occupation O*NET/SOC 19-4044.00, Hydrologic Technicians: collecting and organizing data about groundwater and surface-water distribution and circulation and their physical, chemical, and biological properties; measuring and reporting flow rates and groundwater levels; maintaining field equipment; collecting water samples; installing and retrieving sampling equipment; and processing samples for laboratory shipment. Technicians may collect data for hydrologists, engineers, developers, government agencies, or agriculture. Official scope: Collect and organize data concerning the distribution and circulation of ground and surface water, and data on its physical, chemical, and biological properties. Measure and report on flow rates and ground water levels, maintain field equipment, collect water samples, install and collect sampling equipment, and process samples for shipment to testing laboratories. May collect data on behalf of hydrologists, engineers, developers, government agencies, or agriculture. U.S. wages and employment come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS 2024—2034 employment projections presented by O*NET (specific occupation 19-4044.00). Precise mainland Chinese occupational wages were not obtained and are recorded as a visible gap. The jurisdictions and environmental-protection systems are not interchangeable.

To assess your fit for hydrologic technician work, first complete a verifiable field exercise using public or simulated materials. Set up a fictional monitoring scenario, such as continuously monitoring water levels and flow along a river reach and providing real-time data during heavy rain. Write a step-by-step process from confirming monitoring goals and locations, installing or maintaining water-level recorders and flow meters, collecting water samples and recording physicochemical indicators according to procedures, and conducting data quality control, through organizing data and writing reports or providing real-time data to emergency and weather services. Mark each checkpoint and possible anomaly: equipment failures or abnormal readings, contaminated or improperly preserved samples, missing or out-of-range data, flood-period safety risks, and incompatible data definitions. Afterward, check whether equipment calibration and data quality control, sample preservation and shipment standards, and field safety are mandatory steps; whether environmental conclusions or engineering judgments beyond your authority require consultation or referral; and whether data and processing form reviewable records. Assess yourself through actual deliverables rather than an interest questionnaire alone.

Fit signals | Tasks and work activities for U.S. O*NET 19-4044.00 center on collecting water and soil samples, measuring water levels and flow, installing and maintaining hydrologic equipment, analyzing data and controlling quality, and providing data to hydrologists and relevant departments. Work involves outdoor and waterside fieldwork, equipment maintenance, and sample processing. The interest code is RCI (Realistic—Conventional—Investigative), and work styles emphasize caution, attention to detail, and dependability. If you are willing to operate equipment according to procedures, collect samples, and maintain data quality in outdoor and aquatic environments while prioritizing safety and records, these daily demands may align with your working style.

Caution signals | This O*NET profile is a subset, with data collection underway, and some work-context data have not been published. The official scope and tasks involve outdoor and waterside fieldwork, equipment installation and maintenance, and sample and data quality. An undetected equipment failure or abnormal reading, improper sampling or preservation, missing data quality control, or disregard for field safety during heavy rain or floods may invalidate data, mislead conclusions, or endanger people. This page therefore addresses equipment and calibration, sampling and sample preservation, data quality control, and field safety and authorization boundaries separately. The U.S. occupation itself is not marked Bright Outlook; the O*NET summary projects a decline (-2%) in 2024—2034, about 400 annual openings, and approximately 3,100 employed in 2024. If outdoor and waterside fieldwork, equipment maintenance, or data-quality pressure would be difficult for you, treat them as real costs requiring careful consideration.

Responsibility assessment | Genuine fit depends on whether you can accomplish three things within the same monitoring assignment: carry out fieldwork and data work thoroughly, installing and maintaining equipment, collecting water samples and measuring water levels and flow according to procedures, controlling quality, and organizing data to produce reviewable data and reports; maintain standards and safety through sample preservation and shipment rules, equipment calibration, and field and waterside safety under organizational and regulatory requirements; and accept defined job responsibilities, taking responsibility for the quality of your collected data and records while consulting or referring environmental conclusions or engineering judgments beyond your authority. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as completing a step-by-step monitoring procedure and data log or practicing identification and handling of common equipment and data anomalies, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Hydrologic technicians' daily work can be divided into three strands: (1) fieldwork and equipment—installing and maintaining water-level recorders, flow meters, and water analyzers, and measuring water levels, volumes, and flow rates; (2) sampling and data—collecting water and soil samples and processing them for laboratory shipment, recording and organizing data, and controlling quality; (3) analysis and communication—analyzing environmental data, preparing maps, tables, and reports, and providing real-time data to emergency and weather services during floods and other events. All three share quality and safety requirements but produce different outputs: fieldwork concerns equipment and conditions, sampling and data concern data quality, and analysis and communication concern conclusions and users.

Core tasks include collecting water and soil samples, measuring water levels and flow, preparing, installing, maintaining, or repairing hydrologic equipment, conducting data quality control, developing hydrologic models, and writing reports. Job Zone Three: medium preparation needed.

entries.answer: According to O*NET 19-4044.00, this occupation collects and organizes data on groundwater and surface-water distribution and circulation and physical, chemical, and biological properties; measures and reports flow rates and groundwater levels; maintains field equipment; collects water samples; installs and retrieves sampling equipment; and processes samples for laboratory shipment. Typical tasks include collecting water and soil samples, measuring water levels and flow, preparing, installing, maintaining, or repairing hydrologic equipment, conducting data quality control, developing hydrologic models, and writing reports.
entries.question: What do hydrologic technicians do?

entries.answer: Water resource specialists produce water-resource plans and policy; hydrologists professionally analyze and interpret hydrologic processes; geographic information systems technicians focus on spatial-data processing and mapping; environmental science and protection technicians work with environmental samples and exposure assessments; and water/wastewater engineers handle engineering design and water-treatment systems. Work objects, qualifications, and responsibility boundaries differ; titles are not interchangeable.

subject.name: Hydrologic Technicians
subject.summary: Hydrologic technicians correspond to the specific U.S. occupation O*NET/SOC 19-4044.00, Hydrologic Technicians: they collect and organize data about groundwater and surface-water distribution and circulation and their physical, chemical, and biological properties; measure and report flow rates and groundwater levels; maintain field equipment; collect water samples; install and retrieve sampling equipment; and process samples for shipment to laboratories. They may collect data for hydrologists, engineers, developers, government agencies, or agriculture. Official scope: Collect and organize data concerning the distribution and circulation of ground and surface water, and data on its physical, chemical, and biological properties. Measure and report on flow rates and ground water levels, maintain field equipment, collect water samples, install and collect sampling equipment, and process samples for shipment to testing laboratories. May collect data on behalf of hydrologists, engineers, developers, government agencies, or agriculture. Core tasks include collecting water and soil samples, measuring water levels and flow rates, preparing, installing, maintaining, or repairing hydrologic equipment, conducting data quality control, developing hydrologic models, and writing reports. U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS 2024—2034 employment projections presented by O*NET (specific occupation 19-4044.00). Precise mainland Chinese occupational wages were not obtained and are recorded as a visible gap; China's qualification and environmental-protection boundaries are marked separately.
